speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF VISIT BY PREMIER AND FOREIGN MINISTER OF FRANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be able to inform the house that Mr. Guy Mollet, the prime minister of France, and his minister of foreign affairs, Mr. Christian Pineau, will be flown up to Ottawa from New York on Saturday morning, March 2, and will fly to Quebec on Sunday to return here on Monday morning, after which they will return to Montreal to take off for Paris late Monday afternoon. Mr. Mollet has agreed to address the members of both houses of parliament and it has been arranged that he will do so at 11.30 a.m., Monday, March 4.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH REPRESENTA- TIVES OF EUROPEAN COUNTRIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. In view of the report from Paris that six west European countries have reached agreement for developing atomic power, may I ask the minister if the three representatives of the Euratom group who were in Ottawa last week had discussions with the Canadian government concerning the sale by Canada of uranium or uranium fuel to this group of nations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: URANIUM
subsubtopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH REPRESENTA- TIVES OF EUROPEAN COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government received a visit from three representatives of the countries that make up the European iron and steel community. These are the six countries to which my hon. friend made reference. I had lunch with these men here in Ottawa. They left here to visit Chalk River, and their subsequent conversations were carried on with Mr. Bennett, the president of Atomic Energy of Canada.
As I understand it, the group were interested in several matters. One was the Canadian avenue of approach to the development of atomic power and the other was arrangements for a supply of uranium. However, I am unable to tell my hon. friend of any definite arrangements resulting from their visit.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: URANIUM
subsubtopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH REPRESENTA- TIVES OF EUROPEAN COUNTRIES
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question. If any arrangements are made for the sale of uranium to this group, would the minister indicate to what quantity it might run?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: URANIUM
subsubtopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH REPRESENTA- TIVES OF EUROPEAN COUNTRIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the moment we are prepared to sell only small quantities of uranium outside our present commitments. However, we believe that is all that these countries will require for the time being. It takes two or three years to build an atomic power plant. We believe that by the time they require larger quantities we shall be able to furnish the required quantities.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 19, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Gardiner-Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair:
Prairie Farm Assistance Act That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to increase the awards and the levy authorized by the act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED AWARDS AND LEVY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I must say at the outset that we naturally welcome a resolution which will lead to an amendment of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. For some years we in this group have pointed out to the government some of the very grave injustices and very serious shortcomings in the act in the hope that before this date an amendment would have been brought in. Since 1957 is an election year, I suppose, one of the nice things that the government has presented to the house is this resolution preceding a bill.
Since the purchasing power of the dollar has decreased so seriously under inflation we have constantly advocated an increase in the benefits under the act. We had the minister's assurance yesterday that some increase was contemplated. In so far as there is an increase we will support it. If it turns out to be insufficient I can assure the minister that we shall let him know that we do not think it is sufficient.
The purchasing power of the dollar today in Canada has seriously declined. It has declined to such an extent that you require more than the benefits that you can get from the returns on land which might come under this act to maintain a family or even to get groceries for the family.
I know of actual cases in my own constituency where a young farmer has qualified under the act and then has had his crop completely wiped out through drought. There was certainly nothing coming to him under the P.F.A.A. for some time and he did the best thing he could, he took a job in a neighbouring town and commuted home in the evenings and on weekends to help take care of his farm. But because he did that he was excluded from receiving benefits under the act; he was compelled to do it because the benefits he would have received were so small.
The government can place responsibility for inflation upon nobody else. They were in power ten, years ago when price controls were removed. The spiral of inflation which they assured us would not occur has occurred. Money from such sources as this do not keep men on the farms and therefore the intent of the act is being wiped out.
The bill amending the P.F.A.A. is a minor one and yet we are dealing with an industry in Canada which is sick. Anything short of a real parity price program will not remedy the situation. However that can be discussed under some other resolution or when the minister's estimates are before the house.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act This may be good medicine but I suggest it is like giving aspirin to a man who has had his back broken. Until the basic wrongs of the industry are taken care of agriculture will continue to suffer.
There are some glaring injustices under this act. One section in the act prohibits a person who has purchased crown land to go into farming after a certain date from benefiting under the act if he has a crop failure. It is incredible but it is true that when this person hauls his grain into the elevator he must pay the 1 per cent levy because that is deducted by law, yet that same law prohibits him from benefiting in any way under the act in case he should have a crop failure.
It is quite natural that people in the rest of Canada who would not be eligible for benefits under this act feel that they are paying some kind of subsidy to agriculture, but this man is paying double. He is excluded from the benefits of the act and yet he pays his share of taxation as a Canadian citizen and also pays the 1 per cent levy required by the act whenever he delivers grain. I hope that that injustice will be wiped out.
I have referred to another injustice that exists under the act, that of the person who in order to maintain his livelihood on his farm leaves the farm to earn money elsewhere because the returns are not sufficient for him to maintain himself on his farm. Such a man should not be excluded from receiving benefits when he has a crop failure. The interprovincial farm union recently presented to this government a brief which included reforms and amendments which they felt would improve this act. They suggested an additional section which would give a measure of justice to Indians living on reservations. They asked that Indians be allowed to participate on the same basis as farmers in any other area.
This resolution indicates that the bill to follow does go some little way in wiping out some of the injustices and therefore we will support it. I hope the bill will be in the hands of hon. members shortly. We will be able to discuss it on second reading and therefore I shall reserve any further remarks until the bill is before the house.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE AUTHORIZED AWARDS AND LEVY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I intend to speak only briefly on this resolution. This measure is designed primarily to give a degree of security to the prairie wheat producers. I am sure it will meet with widespread acceptance in Saskatchewan by people of all political affiliations. As you know, the

prairies have always been particularly susceptible to the vagaries of drought, so susceptible in fact that wheat growing is called the greatest gamble in the world.
Hon. members will recall that in the 1930's our farmers on the prairies went through experiences which were almost unbelievable. A terrible drought which lasted for five or six years brought many thousands of farmers to their knees economically. In those days a farmer had to depend completely upon his own resources, and as a consequence a great majority of them were forced to go on direct relief. Most of the residents in these rural areas had to depend on eastern Canada for assistance, even for charity, for their needs in clothing and sometimes in food. The resulting situation robbed the farmers of western Canada in many cases of their dignity, their self-respect and their pride. Many were forced to move to other parts of the country.
These terrible conditions were largely responsible for the growth of the C.C.F. in Saskatchewan. Many people joined the C.C.F., not because they were socialists but rather because they were fed up with the depression conditions which then existed. I recall my own reasoning during that period. I came back to western Canada from university in 1936 when half the population of our province was on relief. I felt that there must be something wrong with a government which would permit conditions of that kind to exist. The C.C.F. was new, its speakers were plausible, and many of us hoped that they had policies which would help the farmer. Unfortunately time and experience have proved us to have been completely wrong.
One of the great virtues of the Liberal party is that it tries to benefit from past experience. It tries not to make the same mistake twice. That is one reason why this legislation is before us today. There are some in the house who have argued that crop insurance is the only answer to the problem of providing security for the western grain farmer. Undoubtedly crop insurance would be an ideal solution. But unfortunately there is not a company in the world, not even Lloyd's of London, which would be willing to assume the risks involved in insuring the western grain crop.
Whether the socialists like it or not, there is no power that the federal government has under our constitution, under which they can introduce crop insurance. That field lies completely within the jurisdiction of our provincial governments. If the socialists feel so strongly that we should have crop insurance, they should appeal to the C.C.F. government in Saskatchewan.
So the Liberal party had to look elsewhere for a solution.

In 1939, largely, I think, at the instigation of the Minister of Agriculture, an alternative to crop insurance was found and the original P.F.A.A. was introduced. Its object was simple and straightforward; it sought to guarantee to the western farmer that no matter how severely he was treated by the vagaries of climate or nature, he would have a certain basic income with which to pay for food and clothing and, perhaps, seed. Under the 1939 act, a minimum payment of $2.50 per acre was provided on half the cultivated acreage up to a maximum of 400 acres, with a total payment not exceeding $500.
Mr. Chairman, this particular act has been to the prairie farmer what the Unemployment Insurance Act has been to the working man. The farmer has borne a part of the cost by paying out one cent a bushel on the wheat he sells, but it is interesting to note that payments to farmers under this act have far exceeded what they have contributed.
Between 1939 and July 1956, prairie producers paid into the fund approximately $95 million. In the same period they have received benefits amounting to $184 million. I think the farmers of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre might be interested to know that they have drawn $6,815,000 under this act. I am sure the people of Assiniboia would be interested in knowing that up to December 31, 1955, they had drawn $13,762,000 under this act.
These substantial payments indicate the value of this Liberal legislation. For a number of years prairie Liberals have realized that the benefits under the act should be extended, and they have consistently urged such action on their colleagues from other parts of Canada. I think the reasons for these representations are fairly obvious. Since 1939 the cost of living has gone up and also the cost of production to the farmer, while inflation has depreciated the value of the Canadian dollar. Now the appeals of prairie Liberal members and, particularly, the appeals of the Minister of Agriculture were made on their merits, in a spirit of reasonableness and co-operation, and this legislation which is before us today is a direct result of those representations.
Under this bill when it is brought down, if my understanding is correct, the benefits will be increased over-all by roughly 50 per cent. Yet the cost to the farmer remains constant. I am convinced, as I said a moment ago, that the farmers of Saskatchewan almost without exception will welcome this measure with open arms. This is particularly true, Mr. Chairman, because of the effects of the great North American drought.
I have talked to many Canadians in recent weeks who have travelled through some of
Prairie Farm Assistance Act the states south of Saskatchewan-Texas, Wyoming, Colorado, Oklahoma-and most of them have been shocked by the devastating effects of that drought. They were shocked by the dust that is flying everywhere, and by the ruin and the desolation which have been caused. It is our earnest hope that this drought will not extend northward into Saskatchewan, yet we know from past experience that this is likely to happen. I say that if a drought does come to Saskatchewan this P.F.A.A. legislation which is now before us, will be one of the major weapons which will be used to fight the effects of that disaster.
I was very interested in C.C.F. criticism of this bill. As they so frequently do, when government legislation is introduced, they announced that they would support it. They dare not do anything else. Then, of course, immediately afterwards they said in effect: "It does not go far enough; a 50 per cent increase in payments is not sufficient; the benefits should be doubled."

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take part in the internecine strife which prevails from time to time between the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre and his opponent the hon. member for Assiniboia. Certainly, what takes place here has indicated that this contest will be one of the most interesting in the province of Saskatchewan, bringing together two redoubtable champions. If this session were to continue at any great length, however, I doubt whether they would have very much to talk about by the time the election came round.
What I rose to say is, simply, this: the introduction of this amendment to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act does meet certain of the objections which have been raised to the act in recent years, and while, no doubt, there are many other changes which could be made and which ought to be made, what is taking place here is a step in the right direction.
We in the prairies, and particularly in Saskatchewan, find ourselves in a position where drought comes to us in periodic cycles. I have been on the prairies since my boyhood. I have seen those successive droughts over

the years in Saskatchewan, particularly, and in parts of Alberta, and I have seen the great distress which they have brought. The Prairie Farm Assistance Act had its inception through the vision of the Minister of Agriculture and what has been done deserves the appreciation of those who live in drought areas.
It operates in part as a counterpart of the legislation introduced under the Bennett regime, the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.
It does seem to me as somewhat of a paradox that we have this legislation before us, necessary as it is, at a time when we find it so difficult to market our production of wheat. Indeed, if the present rate of marketing of the farmers' wheat and the finding of markets abroad continues, the position of affairs at the end of this crop year will result in the amount of wheat on hand being some 628 million bushels compared with 540 million bushels at the end of the crop year, July 31, 1956. That is sometimes rather difficult to understand, and the situation has arisen in considerable part because of the loss of our markets abroad and also by reason of the failure of the government to face up to its responsibilities to make known to the United States of America the complete injustice that is being committed to our agricultural machine by the processes of international marketing being indulged in by the United States.
However that may be, this legislation is necessary. Some discussion took place yesterday on the problem of bringing into effect a system of crop insurance. That idea has been with us throughout the years, and it is a problem that is difficult of solution. One province by itself cannot do so. At least, that was the conclusion arrived at in Manitoba by the royal commission that looked into the matter. Their general conclusion was that at least three provinces would have to join together in order to make such a scheme practicable.
Everyone realizes that the amounts payable under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act are insufficient and do not provide for the farmer that measure of protection provided by the original allowances under the act as it stood in 1939 and as subsequently amended. However, the problem is one that cannot be solved as easily as the simple increase of the amount because to increase the amount that the farmer receives will inevitably result in a very considerable increase in the levy.
My suggestions as to other amendments that might be made are these. First, while the placing of indemnities on an individual farm basis may be impractical, consideration should be given, as far as possible, to the

amendment of the act to provide for the payment of indemnity on a section basis. The need of doubling the indemnities is perfectly clear for the reason that the purchasing power of the dollar has decreased very considerably. Indeed, under the wheat board act of 1935 a floor was placed on wheat at that time of 87J cents a bushel. In order to have the same floor today, on the basis of the present purchasing power of the dollar the floor would be $2 a bushel. In other words, there has been a continual diminishing of the purchasing power of the dollar and for that reason it is necessary to increase the amount payable on the individual indemnity.
The question of crop insurance is one that requires a great deal of investigation. If one reads the report of the Saskatchewan commission on rural questions and the report of the Manitoba royal commission one has some idea of the immensity of the problem and all the difficulties inherent in introducing in our country legislation analogous to that in the United States. While I realize that this parliament is now rapidly approaching its end and it is only a matter of a few weeks before it will cease to exist, even now the committee on agriculture might be convened in order to hear representations, consider recommendations and come to a general decision on this very important matter, for sooner or later it has to be faced.
Third, I suggest that the regulations now in existence should be revamped to a considerable extent. That work could be done by the committee on agriculture. Many people who should be entitled to payment of the indemnities provided under the legislation are denied payment because of a too narrow interpretation under the regulations and under the review sections of the regulations and the act. People who contribute should be entitled to their share of the compensation allowed when loss is sustained.
Sir, the Regina Leader-Post summed up the situation very well as far as Saskatchewan is concerned in the issue of February 11 when it dealt with the prairie dilemma. In part it had this to say:
Rumours persist that the federal government is bringing down legislation to increase Prairie Farm Assistance Act payments. Levies paid by farmers on cash proceeds of their grain deliveries will be raised from the present 1 per cent, it is predicted.
Then it deals with the objections of the people of the province of Manitoba respecting the degree to which they are denied payment under the act although required to contribute to the fund. The editorial points out there are alternative suggestions and goes on to say:
There is no obvious way out of the dilemma of providing a self-supporting subsistence scheme for prairie agriculture which runs the gamut of
Prairie Farm Assistance Act areas which seldom have a crop failure to those which, over the past three decades at least, have harvested relatively few good crops. .	.	. The
solution of this problem apparently will have to be approached from several directions. One obvious step ... is to experiment with a selfsustaining crop insurance scheme to determine if it is feasible in other than the extremely high risk areas.
I believe that is necessary and I believe that if the committee on agriculture were set up even at this late date suggestions and recommendations could be made by the committee which would lay a foundation for the establishment of a crop insurance plan. When it is said that it is not within the constitutional power of the federal parliament to bring in such a scheme, I do not accept that argument as other than a desirable means of escape from the setting up of a scheme so necessary to the agricultural machine not only in western Canada but throughout the country generally.
Finally, the Regina Leader-Post mentions that old perennial the South Saskatchewan river dam. It states:
Another is to change our agricultural economy so that the problem areas, where grain production is extremely hazardous, place greater reliance on other products such as livestock. This is where the South Saskatchewan river development project would be able to play its part in assuring livestock fodder and feed grown under irrigation and water for livestock consumption. Instead of increasing P.F.A.A. subsidies, the federal government might be farther ahead in the end were it to invest the money in construction of the dam.
Certainly the construction of the dam would ensure new hopes in a large area of Saskatchewan in which ever since the days of the historic journey of Archbishop Tache, there have been successive periods and cycles of drought. That area thereby would be taken out of continuing claims under this act. Indeed, statistics were prepared some years ago which indicated that the building of this dam would in a period of 30 years, in the savings made in payments under this act, liquidate in its entirety the contribution required to be made by the federal government for the construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam and irrigation project.
While there is going to be no opportunity at this session to discuss the matter of this project I want to make perfectly clear the stand and the attitude of the Conservative party on it. There has been no deviation since 1945. In each successive election the leaders of this party have advocated the need of this dam which ultimately, by its beneficial effects, would not only obviate the drain on the Prairie Farm Assistance Act fund that today occurs in that area but would assure a diversification of our agricultural economy and would pay dividends beyond

Prairie Farm Assistance Act the imagination of most of us. We stand where we have always stood. We stand in favour of the immediate construction of this irrigation project.
When my friend the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre says that all we have to do is to send down more Liberal members from the province of Saskatchewan in order to achieve beneficial results for agriculture, I ask him simply to recall this fact. On every occasion on which an opportunity has arisen to vote on this irrigation project the Liberal members from the province of Saskatchewan have one and all joined in voting against it.
As far as this resolution is concerned, as has already been stated by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, we intend to support it. It is a step in the right direction. But we believe that in the larger vista of future potentialities for our province, this type of legislation, helpful as it is, merely touches the fringe of the problem. The problem covering a major portion of our province will not be met until that South Saskatchewan river dam and irrigation project has been brought to its completion.

This report is dated Quebec, January 17, and is a report of the proceedings of the house at Quebec appearing in the Gazette. It says this:
Premier Maurice Duplessis today accused the federal government of remaining in the insurance field "in the face of three judgments by the privy council and the Supreme Court of Canada ruling that insurance was under the jurisdiction of the provinces". The premier made the statement before the private bills committee of the legislative assembly during discussion of a bill authorizing the amalgamation of two Quebec insurance companies.
As I said yesterday, I do not claim to be an authority on legal or constitutional questions. I quoted one very prominent Conservative as having held the same opinion I held in the person of Mr. Meighen while he was a member of the other place. Now, I quote another, who is not really a Liberal and I do not know whether or not my hon. friend considers him to be a member of his party. Nevertheless, he is quite a prominent individual in the public affairs of this country. He says that the court has already decided three times that this matter of insurance is under the jurisdiction of the province and not under the jurisdiction of Ottawa. I only repeat that every authority with whom I have ever discussed the matter either in the

147S
Prairie Farm Assistance Act attorney general's department or those who give legal advice on the question of introducing legislation, has maintained that insurance, crop insurance, hail insurance or anything of that kind is a provincial matter. This opinion was given years ago before I entered the legislature of Saskatchewan and resulted in the Saskatchewan government introducing a hail insurance bill. They brought one in in Alberta and in Manitoba, after it had been decided that insurance could not be introduced at Ottawa. I simply say that has always been recognized as a legal decision in connection with the matter. While I acknowledge the very high legal standing of the Leader of the Opposition, I do not think that his opinion could override the courts and others who have given opinions on it.

I take it the bill will be so worded that that will be clearly indicated. I thank the minister for the explanation.
I listened with considerable interest last night. The minister went back to pre-1939 years and discussed conditions which prevailed over a very substantial part of western Canada as a consequence of drought. Many of us do not have to try very hard to recall the situation which existed at that time. Those were particularly grim years. As the minister indicated, there were two complete crop failures during that period.
I also recall hearing him say last night that the heavy relief payments found necessary at that time were destructive of morale. That was undoubtedly true. It resulted in heavy relief expenditures and it certainly discouraged a good many of the farmers and their sons who left the farms. They have not returned. Possibly there are other reasons for it, economic as well as the fact that they have so many memories it has caused them to shy clear of agriculture.

When the act was introduced in 1939, members of the Social Credit party-if the records indicate the true picture, and undoubtedly they do-gave unqualified support to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. We do today. We still feel that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, even with some of the weaknesses that appear in it, is certainly a most desirable piece of legislation, and certainly we feel that the awards under the act should be increased as proposed.
I was also interested last night in hearing the minister emphasize the fact that the act was originally designed to compensate those who suffer crop losses as a consequence of drought. Originally, of course, the act was designed for that purpose. Since then the provisions of the act have been expanded to take in such things as hail, rust and blight. The one complaint that I have always found-and I have given voice to this before -is that the regulations which were designed in the beginning primarily to deal with a drought situation have not been changed sufficiently in their application to hailed-out areas to prevent very serious criticism of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act by people who reside in areas where the only claims which are submitted are submitted in consequence of hail losses. I intend to refer to this in just a moment.
The minister indicated-and I think he went to great lengths to establish the fact -that prairie farm assistance is not crop insurance, it was never intended to be crop insurance, and there is no intention of endeavouring to resolve it into a crop insurance scheme. The minister said-these are not his exact words-the levy was never intended at any time to be a premium paid for insurance. We know that no attempt has been made to make prairie farm assistance an insurance plan; no premiums are paid for the right to draw from the fund. He said-and once again I am not presuming to quote the minister's exact words but just the essence of what he said-that legislation on the statute book was not insurance, was not intended to be insurance and did not have the effect of giving insurance. Now, he emphasized the fact also-and he has done it again today-that constitutionally crop insurance can be set up only by the provinces. Of course, constitutionally that is true; but constitutionally crop insurance on a nation-wide basis and purely on a voluntary basis, as pointed out by the hon. member for Acadia last night, would not involve any constitutional problems whatsoever. In fact, I am personally convinced that crop insurance based on anything less than the entire nation would have about two strikes against it before it ever started. Some have suggested
Prairie Farm Assistance Act that if it were applied to the three prairie provinces there might be a reasonably good chance of its succeeding; but, on the other hand, I personally feel rather dubious of that fact.
In the second place, I feel that if we had it on a nation-wide basis it would offset much of the criticism that is directed toward western agriculture by people living in central and eastern Canada who seem to feel, and often say, that this is just one hand-out after another to western Canadian farmers. I certainly trust that, regardless of whether crop insurance is brought in in any form, regardless of whether there is a constitutional problem-probably I should put it in that way at the moment-the federal Department of Agriculture will continue to do everything it possibly can in co-operation with the provinces, and if the responsibility rests there- and I suggest possibly a good deal of the responsibility rests there quite apart from the constitutional aspect of it-they will never give up the study of crop insurance because certainly, while prairie farm assistance has played a great part in the life of this nation and will continue to do so, it is not crop insurance and cannot serve the purpose of crop insurance. Until we do have a scheme of crop insurance we can hardly expect to have a substantial degree of security or stability in our agricultural industry.
I rose primarily to refer in specific terms to the type of area in which I happen to live and the area which I represent. The minister, of course, is quite familiar with the Red Deer area in central Alberta. It is a very fine mixed farming area. I say it is probably one of the very best mixed farming areas in Canada. It is an area that is not subject to drought. In fact-I may not be right-I have personal recollection of only one township in my constituency that ever qualified for prairie farm assistance because of drought. The losses we have are certain crop losses resulting from early frost in some years, but the main losses suffered in that particular area are hail losses. The year 1957, for example, was a particularly bad year. I would say 1951 and 1952 were the years in which very large sections of that constituency were hit very hard. But even though a very large acreage in that constituency was hit quite hard with hail, it was simply amazing how, under the terms of the act, so many of the farmers in the area failed to qualify for any benefits whatsoever. Now, the major difficulty, of course, results from the very nature of hail itself. In contrast to drought, which usually extends over widespread areas, hail can come in the most peculiar patterns. For example, I can recall at the moment the Pen-hold area where in four successive years hail

Prairie Farm Assistance Act extended over a distance of approximately 40 miles. It averaged probably half a mile in width and caused complete devastation where it hit and yet there was not a single, solitary township in the entire area, so far as I am aware, that qualified for prairie farm assistance in any one of those four years. That type of storm seems particularly peculiar to that area.
Tens of thousands of dollars are paid into prairie farm assistance by the farmers of my area. I have never heard them complain about paying prairie farm assistance; in fact,
I	have heard them say that they would be prepared to pay considerably more provided that the terms of the act were amended to deal with a situation such as that created by those recurrent hail storms.
I have already referred to the fact that in most cases it is very difficult for the townships to qualify. This, of course, is because of the rectangular pattern which must be found, or which must appear, before a block can qualify. There again we are precluded from securing the benefits.
I would like to point out one other thing as well. I am thinking of one particular instance where eight or nine sections of the southern part of the township were just cleaned out, to use a well understood expression, 100 per cent.
We run into extreme figures because in an area like the Red Deer district, if you do not get hail you usually have a heavy crop which boosts the average very high.
Once again I am thinking of that same township I mentioned in the house once before, where 12 sections were hailed out 100 per cent. Under the terms of the act sections 1 to 6 and 7 to 11 received the full benefits, but in section No. 12, which was just as badly hailed as any of the other
II	sections, the three farmers operating there received not one single solitary cent. That section had been drawn up in an irregular pattern which someone had found it possible to form. As the hon. member for Acadia said yesterday, his concern is not so much with the blocks that are brought in as it is with those which by some process of manoeuvring are pulled out of what would otherwise be an eligible area.
I have been told by more than one farmer that they would be prepared to have the levy doubled or tripled if the eligibility could be brought down to a smaller unit. I pointed out that I consider it rather doubtful if it would ever be brought down to the point where benefits would be paid on an individual farm basis, but I said that as far as hail was concerned I could see a good deal of merit in having it paid on the basis

of a section unit. On the basis of my experience I still feel that this would be an excellent method.
In 1953 I had reason to believe that something was going to be done. As I have said, in 1951 and 1952 we had a lot of hail, and then came the election in 1953. Feeling was running pretty high, in fact I said at that time in the house that if there was one single solitary thing that was causing discontent it was the administration of the P.F.A.A. In saying that I am not attacking any official of the department, because after all I realize that they must interpret the regulations as they are placed before them and administer them in as fair a manner as possible.
As I say, I assumed that something was going to be done in 1953 because my Liberal opponent came out with some kind of an election package, but he never took the string off it. The people in my constituency were told that the Liberals had found the answer for the problem that existed in Red Deer constituency, that if they would just elect the Liberal candidate the string would be taken off the package after the election and the problem would be solved. As far as I am concerned the string has never been taken off, and that package is still buried under a not very large pile of minority votes. That is rather unfortunate, though that is probably legitimate politics and I am not complaining from that point of view.
I am suggesting, however, that at that time even the Liberals recognized the seriousness of the problem in that area and the unfairness of the act as it operated there. Of course our hail losses have not been as severe in recent years, and we have not had the same reason to bring forward this matter. But even though the damage may have been less, in view of the facts I have set out I am going to press just a bit harder to have them take off the string. I will be interested in knowing just what the Liberal candidate in my riding will have to offer as a solution to this problem.
When the hon. member for Acadia was speaking the minister made a rather interesting interjection, to be found on page 1435 of Hansard of February 19, as follows:
I will just drop a word now. This Social Credit government of Alberta which is talking about doing something to prevent hail is asking us to help them.
I should like to ask the minister if he has actually had representations from the government of Alberta asking for assistance in provincial hail suppression programs. Experiments are being conducted in that area, and while it is too early to come to any fixed

conclusion it is rather significant to note that in that area which has been blanked out tor years by the line companies as far as hail insurance is concerned, there was a great decrease in the amount of hail which fell during the year. Of course I am prepared to agree that this may be because of the nature of the season itself. However, I am told that an area just outside the area in which the hail suppression program was carried on received the same amount of hail as had been received in the previous year.
As I say, it will probably take several years before they know, but I would say to those who have laughed about this sort of thing that they should reserve their mirth. I rather took from what the minister said last night that in his mind there might be a joke about it.

Perhaps the hon. member will permit me to answer now. The hon. member asked whether the province of Alberta had indicated that they would like to have some help. First may I say that I have had no intention at any time of indicating that there is any mirth in this thing or any reason for laughing about it. Strong representations have been made not only by the provincial government but by the organization which has been set up to promote this battle against hail. I do not know enough about the scientific part of it to say whether they will get anywhere, but I know enough about these things to say that anything of that kind is worth trying until you prove that it will not work.

I am pleased to hear the minister say that, because I have had a number of communications from those who are vitally interested in this hail suppression program. I know they have been particularly interested in securing both provincial and federal help in connection with this project. I know the minister is as interested as I am in anything that might result in less hail falling in any area, particularly in those areas where the damage has been so devastating.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act
I should like to ask the minister if any research has been done on hail suppression by any agency of the federal government. I do not know of any research that is being carried on in Alberta, and I do not know whether the government of Alberta is assisting in the financing of such a project. I hope they are; if they are not, I hope they will, and I say the same thing to the minister as federal minister.
I should like to refer to just one other thing in connection with the P.F.A.A., and I do this because of representations that have been made to me from time to time by farmers who have lost their crops. As the minister knows, hail loss is a pretty devastating type of loss because in many cases you are not even left with feed for your livestock. These people have had to go out and seek temporary off the farm employment. In many cases it has been a matter of whether they eat or do not eat. In my province quite a number of younger people, many of them veterans, have settled on land within recent years.
It is not as if these people had been established for a number of years and had the opportunity of building up a reserve against emergencies. In these cases people have had to leave the farms and make some arrangement to carry on. In one case I know of, the man left his wife and children there so he might go elsewhere to earn enough to pay grocery and other necessary bills. Yet, under the provisions of the act as it stands at present, these people have no protection, and I urge the government to take another look at this matter and give it their serious consideration.
If the Department of Agriculture could see its way clear to changing the unit of eligibility, particularly in relation to hail, and to look into this other matter, namely that of persons who are compelled to seek seasonal work, then I am sure most of the complaints which are directed against P.F.A.A. in my part of the country would be removed. I would also tell the minister this. The farmers with whom I have talked have indicated to me that they are prepared to pay considerably more than they are called upon to pay at the present time. That is virtually the unanimous view expressed to me by farmers with whom I have been in contact.
In conclusion, I would say that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been a very wonderful thing for western Canada. We have supported it in the past and we will continue to support it; and even if crop insurance were brought in there would still appear to me to be a need for such legislation as this. With regard to what the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre said, I do not think his

Prairie Farm Assistance Act comparison between the Unemployment Insurance Act and prairie farm assistance was a good one. Under the Unemployment Insurance Act we do not have to wait until 40 or 50 other people are unemployed before qualifying for benefit; under P.F.A.A. that is what it amounts to. I do not think the two things should be compared. We believe that each, in its own field, does a wonderful job.

Mr. Chairman, I had not intended to take part in the discussion today. I thought perhaps the resolution stage would have been completed yesterday; we could then have had the bill before us in order to see exactly what it means and what it contemplates doing. But the debate did not conclude last night, and I want to make just a few remarks in connection with this legislation.
I was in the house myself in 1938 when this bill first became effective. I have always had a great deal of sympathy with farmers and their agricultural problems, and I knew that western farmers were in rather dire straits as a result of poor crops, so I certainly supported the measure wholeheartedly. But it does seem to me that the situation today is entirely changed; western farmers are not in the same circumstances at all as they were at that time. Consequently I think I should be permitted to put a few facts on the record to indicate, at least to the house, that this legislation as it applies to the three prairie provinces is not so vital today as it was then.
Since 1935 when I first came into this house western wheat growers have had a great deal of assistance from the government, or the consolidated revenue fund, or the taxpayers, whatever you wish. The first provision for prairie farm assistance was brought down as a temporary measure by the Bennett administration. It provided for the spending of $4,750,000 over a five-year period. This measure was to provide for the rehabilitation of the drought and soil-drifting areas of the prairie provinces; it was amended in 1937 and further amended in 1939, when the five-year limitation was removed. The act has been in force in Canada ever since.
My figures are not quite up to date and do not cover the crop year 1955-56, but from 1935 to 1955 approximately $100 million has been spent in the three prairie provinces on P.F.R.A. P.F.A.A. was brought in in 1939, and from 1939 to March 31, 1955, the total amount paid under this act was $177,397,625, less some $85 million recovered from grain delivered collections, leaving a balance of $91,629,692 which was paid by the government.
The wheat acreage reduction plan operated from 1942 to 1946, during which time the government paid to the farmers, for summer fallowing and so on, approximately $90 million. In addition, in October, 1941, order

in council P.C. 8126 authorized $20 million to be paid to western farmers to make up for their lack of income.
During the debate last year on Bills 82 and 83, several speakers sponsoring the interests of western Canada claimed that the wheat board had paid its own expenses and cost the government nothing. Well, how does this work out? Let me read an item from the Canadian wheat board report of 1935-46, reprinted from the Canada Year Book and headed "Operations of the board":
Purchases from the producers during the crop year amounted to 292,360,030 bushels and there was an unsold carryover of 86.539,554 bushels shown at July 31, 1939. This wheat was sold during the following crop year, 1939-40, but the account for the 1938 crop was not closed out until April 24, 1942, when the final funds were received from the Department of Finance. The deficit resulting from the board's operations in 1938-39 was then placed at $61,525,691.
We all remember, of course, the $65 million that was granted in 1951. And now we come to the provision which was made last year, $32 million for wheat storage.
Let me summarize all this and calculate the cost to the taxpayers of this country. P.F.R.A. between 1935 and 1955 cost $100 million; P.F.A.A. since 1939, including the crop year 1945-1955, cost $91 million; wheat acreage reduction from 1942 to 1945, $90 million; prairie farm income, 1941-42, $20 million; subsidy to the wheat board, 1938-39, $61 million; subsidy to the wheat board in 1951, $65 million; payment last year for storage, approximately $32 million, and this year another payment of $32 million. This list does not include payments on account of P.F.R.A. and P.F.A.A. for the crop year 1955, and the total will probably amount to well over $500 million in respect of the years between 1935 and 1955, and for the crop year 1956.
Now, that is not bad. I think that is pretty good. This act which we are amending now does not, it should be remembered, affect any of the farm districts outside the three prairie provinces. It is, actually, in the nature of a crop insurance plan. Now, I do not believe there is anyone in this house who knows the problems of agriculture from one end of the country to the other as well as the Minister of Agriculture. The minister said last night, however, that the distribution of subsidies or grants throughout the provinces was approximately even. Well, I hope when the estimates are under discussion he will show me that this is true, because it is hard for me to believe it.
What I want to point out to the committee is that there are other parts of the agricultural economy which are not so prosperous, either.

Take the province of Ontario. Last year the weather was rather wet and cold. The farmers here grow corn in a big way, but with the wet and cold weather last year the crop did not mature very rapidly. Then there was an early frost and much of the corn did not mature. A lot of it was never harvested at all. There were thousands of acres that were of no value at all from a production standpoint.
Then there is the white bean crop that we have in western Ontario. You must have comparatively dry weather to harvest that crop. We lost most of the bean crop in 1955, and we had no recourse of any kind. When I discussed the matter with the officials of the Department of Agriculture-I am not sure whether or not I got a definite statement from the minister-to see if there was any redress at all I was told it was a purely provincial matter and that the province should take care of it. Last year we had a lot of hail and many farmers lost whole crops of tobacco. If they did not have hail insurance they lost everything.
In the light of these facts do you think it is fair to have a crop insurance plan for the prairie provinces only? You can call it a relief measure, if you will, but it is in the nature of a crop insurance plan. Do you think it is fair to have a crop insurance plan, perhaps not adequate but the nucleus of a plan, for the three prairie provinces which have enjoyed a good deal of prosperity in the last few years, and ask farmers engaged in other types of agriculture in other parts of Canada who do not have a very high income to contribute to the plan? I do not think that is quite fair.
I have tried to get figures from the bureau of statistics to show the amount of income tax paid by farmers, because it is said that income tax collections are some indication of their income wherever they may be. In 1952 the income tax paid by farmers across Canada amounted to $27,454,000. The amount paid by Saskatchewan farmers was $13 million and the amount paid by Alberta farmers was something like $8,350,000. This means that Saskatchewan and Alberta farmers paid approximately $21 million out of the $27 million collected in 1952.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act to hear that there is to be no increase in the amount they will be called upon to pay under the scheme.
In that area, of course, there has been a certain amount of mild grumbling about having to pay for this scheme because of the fact that the farmers are never able to collect anything. A few of them did collect a certain amount three years ago, I believe, when there was very wide hail damage in that area, but apart from hail damage the fact is that in that area, as in quite a number of other areas in Alberta and also in Manitoba, there is no chance of people collecting under the scheme. As I say, there has been a certain amount of mild grumbling, although on the whole the farmers, even though they realize they cannot collect except for hail damage, are agreeable to paying the levy because they look upon the scheme as a good one for the farmers of western Canada as a whole in protecting them against devastating drought conditions or loss of crops otherwise.
The only time any collection was made under the scheme was because of the widespread hail damage I mentioned, and I remember one of my neighbours saying, "Well, it is the most expensive damned hail insurance that anybody could possibly buy." As far as we are concerned that is correct. Having regard to the amount the farmers there have to pay, the amount they can possibly get back by way of return because of hail damage is very small. Nevertheless, in spite of some grumbling the general feeling is that it is a good scheme and there will certainly be no complaint because the payments are being increased. The situation will be the reverse. I think the scheme will be much more acceptable in the part of the country from which I come, and the other areas where the chances of collecting are very small and collection is only made in exceptional circumstances such as hail or flood, because the payments are being increased.
There are some other matters concerning the Prairie Farm Assistance Act in which I am particularly interested, and I wish to refer first of all to the question of lands that are excluded from payment. I would hope that when the act is being amended the minister will take the opportunity to correct some of the injustices as far as payments are concerned. I refer particularly to Indians. In Alberta there are now quite a large number of Indians who are farming on reservations, but they are not eligible for payments under the act. They have to pay into the fund just the same as everybody else, but they cannot collect because they are on a reservation. Some of these Indians cultivate considerable acreages, particularly on the Blood and Blackfoot reserves.


Some of the cultivation carried on by Indians is of a co-operative nature, and co-operatives are definitely included under the scheme. Co-operative farms can collect P.F.A.A. payments, but mission schools for Indians which operate farms are not able to collect. I would hope the minister would amend the act at this time in order to include these people. I can see no reason why Indians should be discriminated against in this way. I was glad to see that in the brief presented to the government by the farm unions, whose representatives are in Ottawa at the present time, one of their recommendations was that Indians on reservations be made eligible for P.F.A.A. payments.
Another group of people whom I can see no reason for excluding are those covered by section 3 of the act, subsection' 3 of which reads as follows:
3. No award under this section shall be made . . .
And this is under paragraph (c) (i).
(i) lands disposed of to a settler or veteran under the Soldier Settlement Act, chapter 188 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, or the Veterans' Land Act . . .
Why people who hold land under the Soldier Settlement Act or under the Veterans' Land Act should be excluded from the benefits of this act I quite fail to understand. It seems to be another case of gross discrimination for which there is no excuse. I would make a very strong plea to the minister that he remove that exclusion from the benefits of this act as far as people holding land under the Veterans' Land Act are concerned. As a matter of fact the amount of land any veteran was able to get under the Veterans' Land Act was a small farm, not sufficient to put him in farming in a very big way. They are among the very group of farmers who on the whole perhaps need the assistance or help they can get under a scheme of this kind more than do farmers generally.

Mr. Chairman, now that nearly all the trumpets have sounded from the prairie provinces I think it is only fair that I should have the opportunity to blow a few piccolo notes on behalf of the fruit growers of British Columbia. I hope to make some brief and, I trust, appropriate remarks in presenting their views with respect to the question of insuring growers against the hazards of damage to crops. Other members of our group are much more competent than I to deal with the grain aspect of the situation from their personal experience and knowledge. I just want to take the opportunity under this resolution, as others have done, to present the views of a good number of people whom I have the honour to represent.
Like the other members of this group I support the bill in principle as a step in the right direction to assist those who need assistance and to meet what I presume is considered a somewhat particular situation, definitely related to the hazards of growing grain under certain conditions. However, as far as the growers of British Columbia are concerned this type of legislation, while it meets certain situations, does not meet the needs of the farmers generally in Canada, and the question of devising some scheme to meet those needs has been under discussion by the British Columbia fruit growers' association over a good number of years.
In British Columbia, as far as the tree fruit industry is concerned, we are subject to two particular hazards. The first is hail damage to fruit on the trees and the second is frost damage to the trees themselves. The first occurs in some areas possibly to some extent nearly every season. The second happens only over long periods of time. It happened in the winter of 1949 and 1950 when the growers of British Columbia suffered serious loss as a result of frost injury to trees, as a consequence of which they were obliged to pull out a great many of those trees and lost the crop not only for the next year but for a good number of years.
As the minister knows, they made application to this government for assistance, and that assistance was denied. I have never been quite able to understand why there is a different approach to these applications for assistance from various parts of Canada. I think agricultural producers should be treated on the same basis. As a result of the situation that has existed throughout the years the growers of British Columbia

Prairie Farm Assistance Act have come to the conclusion that the problem will not be solved satisfactorily until we have some form of national crop insurance. I can see the minister's interest in the growers of British Columbia when I look at his back.

speechtext:
I think it is only fair to the growers, in view of the close study they have given to this question, that I should say this. They have had a committee studying this problem of a national crop insurance scheme for a number of years. It is not a question of just getting up and making off the cuff statements and things of that sort. They have realized all the difficulties. They have realized the need of the farmers generally in this respect and the problems related to it.
This committee, made up of fruit growers, reported to the 1955 convention of the British Columbia fruit growers' association. As a result of that report there was presented to the convention a resolution which was adopted, and I am going to read the resolution into the record because I think it offers a constructive approach to what I admit is an extremely difficult problem that is facing agriculture in Canada at this time.
This is the resolution. It is somewhat lengthy, but in view of the thought given to the matter I think it is worth putting on the record. This resolution was presented toy the executive of the British Columbia fruit growers' association on behalf of the crop hazards committee.
This was the name of the committee that gave a great deal of study to this question, studied all angles of it such as the growing angle, the weather angle, the financial angle, and all the rest of it.
Whereas the crop hazards committee was appointed to report on the feasibility of providing some form of insurance or of setting up reserves against frost and other crop hazards beyond the control of growers, and
Whereas this committee has recommended three methods by which presently un-insurable crop hazards, beyond the control of the growers, could be provided for,
Therefore, be it resolved by this 1955 B.C.F.G.A. convention:
A.	That this association support the principle of a national system of voluntary crop insurance embracing all sections of agriculture, and that we work through the Canadian federation of agriculture to have a scheme to provide such insurance enacted by the federal government at the earliest possible time.
B.	That pending the establishment of a national scheme as outlined in section A, the executive, B.C.F.G.A., be instructed to seek the co-operation and assistance of the provincial and federal governments in establishing a voluntary and contributory crop insurance scheme on an industrywide basis under government supervision and with government financial assistance similar in principle

to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, but with the proviso that before such scheme shall be implemented a plebiscite shall be taken of all growers and a majority of at least two-thirds of those voting shall be required to be in favour before the scheme becomes operative.
C.	That pending the establishment of either of the above schemes, the executive, B.C.F.G.A., be instructed to sponsor and assist in the formation of a separate association for purposes of collecting a crop hazard fund by means of voluntary box deductions under a separate and special contract brought up for that purpose; such association to be administered quite separately from the B.C.F.G.A., with its own officers and a membership consisting of contract holders only and with benefits confined to contract holders, and that with the proviso that until and unless two-thirds of the presently registered growers have agreed to participate in such a scheme and have signed a five-year contract to that effect such scheme shall not become operative.
The result of the resolution was, first of all, that they made representations with respect to sections A and B of the resolution for the establishment of a national voluntary contributory scheme on an agricultural industry basis. Then, as usually happens with the growers in British Columbia, they got to work on their own behalf and organized a hail insurance company. This has been functioning quite well up to the present time. At the same time the growers recognize it is only an expedient that can assist only one group of agricultural producers and deals particularly with one type of damage to crops, hail damage.
The question of crop insurance has also been under consideration in the United States, as the minister knows, for quite a number of years. There is a very successful scheme in operation over there so it is not, as the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre implied, something that is unsound financially, which cannot be organized on a sound basis. It has been organized on a sound basis and given effect in the United States. It has been organized to a lesser degree by the fruit growers of British Columbia.
I listened with great interest this afternoon to the remarks made by the Leader of the Opposition when he was making his plea with respect to a crop insurance scheme in Canada. He was of the opinion that such a scheme, when organized by the federal government, was not unconstitutional. I am not an authority on the constitutional aspects of the question, but I do suggest it is up to the federal government to take the initiative in this matter, to give some lead. They have the machinery for doing so. The minister should do that and try bringing this question to the attention of the next dominion-provincial conference on agriculture. I admit the difficulties, and I admit it would take some time to study and establish.

There are a number of things to be considered if the scheme is going to be organized to the satisfaction of the farmers and at the same time on a sound basis.
But I do urge him to give this matter consideration and to take the initiative in bringing it before the next dominion-provincial conference on agriculture. There is no doubt it will require careful study. It will require the co-ordination of agricultural activities across Canada, and it will require the co-operation of all the provinces.
I think it is generally recognized that, while the minister says this is a provincial responsibility from a constitutional point of view-he may be correct on that point-such a scheme cannot be organized on a provincial basis. It is generally understood by those who have studied the scheme closely that it would have to be organized on a national basis if it were to be sound and satisfactory. I do urge the minister to give consideration to taking the initiative in the development of a national crop insurance scheme, and in so doing give the opportunity of bringing the magic law of averages to the rescue of thousands of farmers in this country.

I merely mention this because I think it emphasizes the need for a national crop insurance scheme which would operate right across Canada in order to get away from this type of criticism. As it is, every time legislation is brought in which deals exclusively with western Canada there will always be that type of criticism from a few members and, as we know, a number of hon. members who do not voice that sort of criticism feel it, nevertheless.
The minister has suggested that we should perhaps undertake a crop insurance scheme in one of the provinces in western Canada.


The hon. gentleman has a very high opinion, I know, of the views expressed by the late Mr. Motherwell. The report he made stresses that in his opinion crop insurance should be brought in as a federal scheme, and could not be successfully undertaken by individual provinces.

Surely the Minister of Agriculture is not going to suggest that we have got ourselves in such a strait jacket in this country that if the provinces want it and the federal government wants it we are not able to bring a nation-wide crop insurance scheme into effect.
I think the minister would agree that if we are to introduce a nation-wide crop insurance scheme it should be done in conjunction with the federal government. It would not be wise just to have the provinces try to do it independently of one another. It has to be done on some basis through the federal government. I think that is the only way we can get away from the kind of criticism we heard from the hon. member for Lambton-Kent.

Mr. Chairman I did not think the hon. member wanted a reply to the first question he asked before sitting down. I thought he was simply making a point and I suggested to him that we could discuss it better on the bill when we know what is in the bill. I only want to repeat what I said previously and what I think I can maintain when we get on the bill itself, that this legislation as it is now drafted takes at least as good care of the farmer as the 1939 legislation did of the farmer in those days. That is as far as I am going to go at the moment on that matter.
As to the other question, there is a long list of persons who are not paid under the act. As I said earlier, in referring to one of the members of the official opposition, there are about 20 different groups. There may be more than that. I see there are 14 classifications with half a dozen in each of two or three of them, and there would easily be 20 altogether. One person whom I think everybody would admit should not be eligible is the man who owns land and lives outside the country, and also the man who lives in some other province. He may live in eastern Canada or in British Columbia and not live in the area concerned at all. These categories are ruled out.
Then we have the man who is teaching school. There was some argument back and forth with respect to such a person from the point of view of whether he was getting enough to carry him through any difficulties that might arise, and I think he does. Then there is the man who runs an elevator and is paid a salary for handling the grain of the farmers who are being assisted. Then you come to the storekeeper who has a farm outside the village and also runs a store. The objective of the act is to help to get his accounts paid. One can go through the whole list and find that what the act attempts to do is to keep people in that area.
There were a million people living in the area we are most concerned about at the time the legislation was first introduced. Over the whole area there were many more than that, but there were a million in the area we were most concerned about, and the idea was to try to keep them there until they could learn to farm in that area in a way that would make it possible for them to maintain themselves. It was said that it was not necessary to assist the teacher that these very farmers were paying, that it was not necessary to assist the merchant there to whom they would probably pay all the money they received. It is not necessary to pay a man who has a job of any kind which gives him payment for his complete time. He is not a farmer.

All I should like to say at the moment is that the legislation will be open for discussion when we go into committee on the bill after second reading, and it will also be open for discussion in the committee on agriculture. All these points can be discussed then; and in answer to the suggestion that we should call certain people here, I hope there will be enough of the people there who have been doing a lot of talking out west so they will learn once more what they have learned on three or four previous occasions and then have gone home and said nothing about it for four or five years. They will learn what the reasons are.
I can think of the time when we had the 400 farmers down here. This was the main question about which they were concerned, and before they left the city of Ottawa they reported that they were in favour of what was being done. No matter how many come here now, I think it will be found that they will report that these are very reasonable provisions.
Finally, may I point out that all we are asking at the moment is what is in the report on crop insurance made by the Saskatchewan commission. They wind up their comments on the P.F.A.A. by saying:
Whatever developments take place in crop insurance, a revamped P.F.A.A. will still be required. During the lengthy transition period necessary to develop and extend crop insurance to its practical limits, P.F.A.A. protection will be essential for those farms not covered. Beyond that period, P.F.A.A. can be envisaged as a permanent relief program for uninsurable farms in high risk areas. Thus, P.F.A.A. and crop insurance would be complementary but separate programs.
That is their opinion. They say the P.F.A.A. not only should continue while crop insurance is being considered, but should continue even after you get crop insurance, if you get it. That being so, why have such a complete discussion on crop insurance when we are talking about this bill? So far as I know, everyone who has been discussing the question, even my friend who has been criticized by the member for Assiniboia, feels that if we could have some kind of crop insurance that would be effective right across the country it would be helpful. We all agree with that, but why go on discussing the question in relation to this legislation when everyone agrees that even if you had crop insurance you would still need to have this legislation? I suggest that we proceed and get the legislation before the house so we will know exactly what we are talking about, and then discuss these other questions in relation to it.

I have one question. While the minister is on the subject of these various categories which are not eligible for P.F.A.A., there was one particular category I had hoped he would mention but he did not do so. I would rather have it all in the same day's discussion. I refer to the group mentioned by the hon. member for Yorkton this afternoon, namely the people who are settled on crown lands. The act at the present time excludes those who purchased crown lands since January 1, 1940, with the exception of those settled under the Veterans' Land Act. I think they have a legitimate grievance there. They are farmers. They do not fall into any of these other categories the minister mentioned, such as wage earners and so forth. Their whole income is from the farms. They are paying the 1 per cent levy. They are not exempt from that, yet they are exempted or excluded from the benefits.
If I understand the situation correctly, that provision was arrived at by agreement with the provinces. A great deal has happened since 1939. I think now there are many cases


where lands which may not have been considered as suitable for grain farming or may have been considered to be submarginal or marginal are not considered in that category today with developments that have taken place. I would hope the minister would give us some hope and encouragement that changes will b.e made in that respect. These farmers are paying their levy year after year and have been doing so since 1939. Then when they have a crop failure, even if they are included in a block in which their neighbours on one side, and sometimes on all sides, are eligible, because of that exclusion they find that they cannot share in the benefits. I think it is a real grievance about which something should be done.

Mr. Chairman, again I would prefer to discuss that matter in committee, but I can give a short answer to that question.
At the time that was put into the act, when we amended it some years ago, that question was put before the committee. As was said by the hon. member for Assiniboia when he was discussing the matter this afternoon, quite a number of things were put into the amendment that were not in it when it was introduced to the committee. One of them was with regard to the group mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Calgary North, I think it was; that is, that returned soldiers should be allowed to settle on this land.
The reason for raising the question at the time was that it had developed that there was one township in Saskatchewan where there were some 34 persons who had gone back on the land in an area that was not considered suitable for agriculture. The bill definitely states that on any submarginal land or land that is declared submarginal we should not make payment. When it was found that people were going in, some examination was made into how they got into that position. It usually turned out that there was some farmer who was farming near the edge of an area such as that and he had maybe one or two sons or some other persons in whom he was interested, and the farm was extended out into that area so that it came in. But it had some effect upon the provision with regard to 400 acres and so on, where a man can only draw on 200 acres. By splitting it up in certain ways three or four may draw instead of one. That was the difficulty that an attempt was made to overcome.
As has been said by the hon. member for Dauphin, the question was fully discussed with representatives of the provincial governments here and all those matters were considered. Then everybody said: All right.

We hear claimed if they came in since 1940 the provincial governments put them on the land after that time. In the 1930's the lands were turned over to the provinces and from 1940 on those persons who were there on the land were there, if it was crown land, with the consent of the provinces. If the provinces consented to their going on it, then they should put them on it under conditions that would make it possible for them to live there. If the lands were considered to be submarginal, then they should not be put there at all.
That was the nature of the argument. So the provincial feeling was, "That is all right provided you exempt certain portions." The special areas that had been mapped out in Alberta were one portion. I think it was the hon. member for Acadia who put forward the argument at that time that these districts should be treated a little bit different. They are so treated by the act. Then somebody said the returned soldier should be treated differently, so the returned soldier was exempted from it. So if he went on the land he could still go on that kind of land and we would pay.
Representations have been made to me to the effect that practically all these lands are now occupied by returned soldiers, and that there is no reason for having this amendment in the act at all. They say that returned soldiers have got into practically all that land under this exemption that is put in the act to provide for a returned soldier getting on it. I have said, "That matter must be investigated before we take this out of the act. If that is the case, there is no good reason for having this still in the act." It is just another indication of how difficult it sometimes is to do things that you think ought to be done when you are dealing with human nature.
