subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND BENEFITS AND PROVIDE CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Is the minister proposing to add anything to what he said on Friday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND BENEFITS AND PROVIDE CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND BENEFITS AND PROVIDE CHANGES IN ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
I think this measure
should be regarded as of very great importance, but nothing the government have done makes me think that they so regard it. I was going to say that this was a step forward, but I think I would not make such a positive statement as that. I think it is a creeping shuffle forward. I think the government is dealing with this in a grudging way, and that it is another instance of too little and too late. They are really just nibbling at what I consider to be a very important subject.
The minister, in speaking about it on Friday last, gave us very much the "mixture as before". He indicated that there was very little the government was going to do about it. Perhaps it is not surprising that

the minister did that because it is only a little more than a year ago that the Prime Minister, in speaking about this matter, referred to it in such terms as to indicate that the government was not taking it very seriously. On page 49 of Hansard for January 12, 1956, the Prime Minister said:
In general, we did not see any need to share In the normal costs of growth of provinces and municipalities. The financing of this growth presented problems, but they did not seem to us to require a federal solution.
The minister himself on Friday last followed along in the same vein by saying this, as recorded at page 1354 of Hansard for February 15, 1957:
Much of the argument advanced for the extension of the program-
That is the program of making payments in lieu of taxes.
-has been on the ground of municipal fiscal need, but this is a provincial matter and not the purpose of a bill of this nature. What we are concerned with here is the effect of the location of federal property within a municipality upon its capacity to perform its proper functions.
Later on the minister gave us a brief history of what had been done over the years, beginning in 1950-51 when the government first made this concession, and continuing up to the present. The amount paid in 1951 was roughly a million and a half, and it has gone up gradually until in 1955-56 it was nearly $7 million and it is estimated that under the present further concession it will rise in the current year to $9,590,000.
The concession now being made, as the minister pointed out, is that the government proposes to remove the 2 per cent floor and pay grants to municipalities with federal property where the normal municipal services in that municipality are performed on account of the federal property. This means that the federal government will, subject to certain exceptions, pay the equivalent of full municipal taxes, including school taxes, on its land and buildings in municipal areas.
As I said a moment ago, Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the government is not dealing seriously with a serious problem. I shall try to give evidence which I hope will satisfy the committee, and which they have often had before, that the municipalities are really up against very great problems and, as I said a moment ago, this is just a nibble. The government proposes an increase which will amount to some $6 million to $10 million, and as hon. members will bear in mind that is not more than one five hundredth of the government's total expenditures, which are about $5,000 million.

We on this side are not in the habit generally of asking for additional expenditures, but there are times when one has to point out that certain expenditures do require to be made, and to suggest with all the vehemence of which we are capable that there are plenty of cases where profusion could be cut down and the result would far more than cover the amount that is needed. I say that to hide behind, pirouette behind, the excuse that this is a provincial matter and therefore the federal government does not deal with it seems to me to be just ignoring the facts.
I would like to put forward on what a former leader of this party once called "the immortal grounds of common sense" the fact that this is a problem which we do not get away from by just shutting our eyes and saying it does not exist.
I would like to digress for a moment and draw attention to the position of crown corporations. We have not only the government's own buildings but we have the buildings of the emanations of the crown, namely crown corporations. The situation there is very unsatisfactory also. They are playing a kind of hide and seek or cat and mouse business with the municipalities, and I would like to put before the committee, because it is an integral part of this problem, what the Minister of Finance said about crown corporations in 1952. At page 1253 of Hansard, of 1952, Mr. Abbott said:
An interesting change I am proposing under the corporation income tax is that those crown corporations of the federal government which are designated as proprietary corporations-
And this is one of them. I continue:
-and hitherto have been exempt from tax, will in future pay corporate income tax to the federal government in the same manner as any privately-owned corporation. "Proprietary corporations" are those so designated under the Financial Administration Act, and generally speaking are companies which are carrying on business operations similar to and in competition with private business. One desirable result of this proposed action will be to make the financial statements of these crown companies more comparable with private industry, and make it easier to assess the relative efficiency of their operations. I do not expect this change to have appreciable net revenue effects. It will increase our tax receipts and reduce our non-tax revenue.
In other words, what you lose on the swings you get on the roundabouts. I continue:
All crown company profits eventually find their way into the treasury, and many of them already remit all or the greater part of their profits year by year.
Now, that seemed to me good sense; yet it has not been carried out. I refer to an item in the Ottawa Journal of February 5, 1957,
Municipal Grants Act
which shows the way in which crown corporations are being allowed to operate and the extent to which this forthright, clear-cut and reasonable proposal of the minister of finance in 1952 has not been carried out. I quote from the Journal:
City treasurer Lowther reported today he had successfully negotiated a $2,670 increase in the 1956 "tax grant" made to Ottawa by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, a crown corporation.
He also reported to board of control that for the first time, a "tax-grant" would be received from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in respect to its Ottawa operation of CBOT at Tunney's pasture.
Mr. Lowther stressed that "tax grants" to Ottawa by crown corporations were a matter of separate negotiation in each case, and every year.
Farther on we find the following:
At present, the C.N.R., the Bank of Canada, and Atomic Energy Limited are paying the equivalent of full municipal taxes, both on real property and business tax.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation had been "negotiated" into paying the equivalent of real property taxes, but disclaimed any business tax obligation. The C.B.C. argues similarly.
And later again:
Mr. Lowther said the dominion government would never pass legislation admitting any liability for such taxes. It would be contrary to the fundamental principle that crown holdings were tax-exempt. However, more and more crown corporations were beginning to admit their "moral obligations".
It seems to me to be more than almost an impertinence for them to come along and say they have nothing but moral obligations. The Minister of Finance said they would pay like anyone else.
Then I read the last paragraph:
Similar business-tax arguments were being pressed with respect to C.M.H.C. and C.B.C., but as yet, they have held out against such obligations.
I think, Mr. Chairman, the question is whether or not the government is really taking this seriously. As I have looked at the action over the years I have wondered-and I can only wonder because I have never been in power myself-whether they like to have the provinces and municipalities in the position where they have to come more or less as suppliants every year. I wonder whether it is conceivable that power does that to people, and that they refuse to deal with this thing and pretend it does not exist year after year, with the municipalities coming and making most convincing arguments, as I shall hope to show. The Gordon report, which we have just received, endorses what I have to say, indicating that the government should pay the equivalent of its taxes and also indicating that there is a big problem for consideration and settlement among the three levels

Municipal Grants Act
of government. I shall also quote from tax authorities pointing out what is being done, and I shall try, with what little hope I am able to summon up, to make the Department of Finance and, through them, the government, feel that the time has come to deal with this as a serious problem, because it is a serious problem.
Will you call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
Progress reported.
